Regarding FTP3 extension with multiple packet sizes:
The number of packet sizes X = 2;
For each packet size S_i, the packets arrive according to Poisson distribution (as FTP 3) with mean inter-arrival time T_i  (or arrival rate λ_i where T_i = 1/ λ_i);
For Alt1: Y=1 packet size is simulated for each UE
For FTP3-extension with X=2, K is the ratio between arrival rates of the packet sizes, i.e., λ_1= K·λ_2, with K>=1, assuming S_1<S_2,
G>=1 is the ratio between the number of UEs with packet size S_1 and S_2, respectively.
Values of S_i, λ_i, i=1, 2, and G can be decided in evaluation phase.
Note: The following table is an illustration of the traffic configurations.
|  | Example 1 | Example 2 | Example 3 |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Packet Type | Small size, i=1 | Large size, i=2 | Small size, i=1 | Large size, i=2 | Small size, i=1 | Large size, i=2 |
| S_i | 10KB | 500KB | 4KB | 400KB | 10KB | 100KB |
| λ_i | λ_1= K·λ_2, e.g., K=[3, 5, 8, 10] |  |  |  |  |  |
| G | N_1= G·N_2, e.g., G=[2, 4, 9] |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | N_1 is the number of UEs with small packet size S_1; N_2 is the number of UEs with large packet size S_2. |  |  |  |  |  |
For Alt2: Y=X=2 packet sizes are simulated for each UE
The packet of each size is generated following the independent Poisson Process (S_i, λ_i) with i=1,2.
K is the ratio between arrival rates of the packet sizes, i.e., λ_1= K·λ_2, with K>=1, assuming S_1<S_2.
Values of (S_i, λ_i) with i=1,2 can be decided in evaluation phase.

For the base graph of LDPC extension beyond NR range, the following is identified in RAN1#124 for further study
The LDPC extension is quasi-cyclic LDPC codes, the parity check matrix of quasi-cyclic LDPC Codes is defined at least by a matrix H of size (mb×z)×(nb×z), which consists of sub-block matrices of size z×z, where each sub-block matrix is composed by circularly shifted matrices or zero matrices. Wherein, mb, nb and z are integers larger than 1.
The values of mb, nb and z are FFS.
The row weight of circularly shifted matrices is less than or equal to 2.
FFS: Whether row weight of all circularly shifted matrices is 1, or the row weight of some circularly shifted matrices is 1 and the row weight of some circularly shifted matrices is 2.

For study of LDPC extension beyond NR range, at least the following metrics are considered for the performance comparison among BG1 and BG(s)/PCM(s) proposed by companies

SNR performance difference with the same computation complexity as BG1 under the reference maximum number of iterations of BG1.
The reference maximum number of iterations is 5, 7, 10, 15 based on BG1.
Other values can be also reported by companies
Note: Companies can report the average number of iterations difference to achieve the same performance as BG1 under the reference maximum number of iterations of BG1.

agenda_title: NTN specific requirements and design for GNSS based operation
text_en:
RAN1 to use the following terminology when discussing GNSS availability at least for physical layer operation.
GNSS-based: Refers to the network mode of operation which relies on devices being equipped with a GNSS receiver and the devices can obtain a position fix within a given accuracy (e.g. 50m)
FFS: How often the UE may be required to obtain a position fix, which may be related to the required accuracy.
FFS: if position under this operation can be obtained by means other than GNSS that provides a comparable accuracy, e.g. pre-configuration for a fixed device. This may also include information other than positioning.
GNSS-degraded: Refers to the network mode of operation which relies on devices being equipped with a GNSS receiver, the devices were able to obtain a position fix at some point in time, but the devices may not currently have a position fix within a given accuracy (e.g. 50m) at the current time.
NOTE: The UE may be able to use the position fix for physical layer operation
GNSS-free/GNSS-less: Refers to the network mode of operation which does not rely on devices being equipped with a GNSS receiver, or devices are equipped with a GNSS receiver but do not have a current position fix that can be used for physical layer operation.

agenda_title: NTN specific requirements and design for GNSS based operation
text_en: 6GR NTN targets to support GNSS-based operation, GNSS-degraded operation and GNSS-less/GNSS-free operation.

agenda_title: NTN specific requirements and design for GNSS based operation
text_en:
6GR NTN uplink time-frequency synchronization follows the same principle as NR NTN as baseline:
The concept of “uplink synchronization reference point” is introduced in 6GR NTN.
6GR NTN provides satellite assistance information
At least for GNSS-based operation, it is supported that UE uses its own location information + satellite assistance information to perform time-frequency pre-compensation.

agenda_title: NTN specific requirements and design for GNSS based operation
text_en:
6GR supports large scheduling offsets to accommodate the RTT introduced by the satellite channel. Further discuss how to realize these scheduling offsets:
Option 1: Reuse the k_offset concept from NR as a baseline with potential modifications.
NOTE: Under this option, additional scheduling offsets (e.g. similar to K1/K2 in NR) may be supported for scheduling flexibility, which apply in addition to k_offset.
Option 2: The large scheduling delays to accommodate the RTT are incorporated into the scheduling offsets (e.g. similar to K1/K2 in NR), which may or may not be common for TN and NTN.

agenda_title: NTN specific requirements and design for GNSS based operation
text_en:
Study NTN specific issues/requirements at least for the following aspects for 6GR NTN under this agenda:
Uplink time-frequency synchronization
HARQ issues: e.g. enable/disable HARQ feedback (which may include how to efficiently operate with HARQ feedback enabled/disabled), number of HARQ processes, etc.
Timing relationships with large RTT.
Coverage target
Physical layer aspects of multi-satellite operation (including multi-orbit)
Aspects related to Multiple beams per satellite
Aspects related to satellite having more beam footprints than simultaneously active beams
Other aspects are not precluded.

text_en:
As a general principle for 6GR NTN study:
Under NTN agenda item, we will identify issues / requirements specific to NTN.
Potential solutions to these issues / requirements may be studied under the NTN agenda
The outcome of this study may be discussed under other agenda items if common design is possible.
These solutions may end up resulting in an extension of the TN design.
This may depend on the solution / issue / requirement
NTN specific solutions may be introduced when a common / extended design cannot meet the NTN requirements.
When targeting a common design TN performance is prioritized.

The payload size estimation of each measurement level/option for NR ISAC can be done by the following formulas
Level A: Msubcarrier* Ncpi *Mtxport*Nrxport*Ntrp*(Nquan1+ Nquan2)
Where,
Msubcarrier: number of subcarriers in a OFDM symbols
Ncpi: number of OFDM symbols within CPI
Mtxport: number of reference signal antenna port for sensing purpose
Nrxport: number of Rx antenna ports
Ntrp: number of TRPs for payload size calculation
Nquan1: number of quantized bits for amplitude
Nquan2: number of quantized bits for angle
Level B:
Delay-Doppler Profile: Mdelay *Ndoppler *Mtxport* Nrxport *Ntrp *(Nquan1+ Nquan2)
Delay-angle Profile: Mdelay * Ncpi *Mtxport*Nangle *Ntrp *(Nquan1+ Nquan2)
Delay-Doppler-angle Profile: Mdelay *Ndoppler *Mtxport*Nangle *Ntrp *(Nquan1+ Nquan2)
Delay Profile: Mdelay *Ncpi*Mtxport*Nrxport *Ntrp *(Nquan1+ Nquan2)
Where,
Mdelay: number of delay samples in the window
Ndoppler: number of Doppler samples in the window
Nangle: number of angle samples in the window
Level C:
C1/C2/C3: Np1*Ntrp *
C4/C5: Np2*Ntrp *
Where,
Np1 is total number of paths
Np2 is total number of points
Nparam is 5 including e.g.,
C1/C3/C4: delay, Doppler, horizontal angle, vertical angle, power measurement
C2/C5: position (x, y, z), radial velocity, power measurement
Nquan,i: number of quantized bits
Ntrp: number of TRPs for payload size calculation
Level D:
Nobject*Ngnb * for options D1/2
Mpoints* Ngnb * for options D3/4
Where,
Nobject is total number of targets
Mpoints is total number of scattering points of all targets
Ngnb is fixed to 1

The study on the following listed proposals is noted. Further discussion on these is not planned under the waveform agenda item in RAN1 unless tasked by RAN at or after RAN#112.

Max-rank = 2 for UL DFT-s-OFDM
Companies report negligible SNR loss from DFT-s-OFDM with larger number of aNB Rx antenna elements, such as at least 16 or 32. Link level loss with 4 layers has not been studied. A lower number of aNB antenna elements may result with SNR loss at the receiver
All companies acknowledge that when the UE is Tx power limited, there is a Tx power gain from DFT-s-OFDM, highest reported gain of around 2.5dB.
The system level impact depends on scenario and scheduling strategy due to vastly differing probabilities for UE to be power limited and use rank=2, as well as the used traffic model and the assumed number of aNB Rx antenna elements. The reference setup to compare with varied and had also an impact to the findings, including also system loading, link adaptation, scheduling strategy, the used UE antenna model and the number of aNB Rx antenna elements.
Two companies reported cases with average system level throughput loss [R1-2601827, R1-2602177], of which one company indicated cell edge throughput loss [R1-2602177]. One company reported no average and cell-edge system level throughput gain [R1-2602254], while 6 companies reported cases with average system level throughput gains and/or cell edge throughput gains [R1-2602004, R1-2603056, R1-2602468, R1-2603008, R1-2603286 , R1-2601921].
Codebook for multi-layer UL DFT-s-OFDM
The lower PAPR property of DFT-s-OFDM is diminished with coherent precoders due to mixing of two (or more) layers for each power amplifier.
RAN1#124 agreed to focus the DFT-s-OFDM studies to non-coherent CB only (with the exception of lower number of layers than Tx antennas) for 2Tx UE for waveform evaluation purposes.
Four companies report moderate system level gains for DFT-s-OFDM non-coherent codebook only relative to CP-OFDM non-coherent codebook [R1-2603056, R1-2602468, R1-2603008, R1-2603286], while two companies report system level loss for DFT-s-OFDM non-coherent codebook only relative to CP-OFDM non-coherent codebook [R1-2601827, R1-2602177].
One company reports system level gains also for DFT-s-OFDM with coherent codebook relative to CP-OFDM with coherent codebook [R1-2602468].
Six companies report system level gains for DFT-s-OFDM with non-coherent multi-layer codebook and coherent single-layer codebook relative to CP-OFDM with coherent single/multi-layer codebook [R1-2602426, R1-2602468, R1-2602004, R1-2603008, R1-2603286, R1-2601921], while one company reports no system level gain for DFT-s-OFDM with non-coherent multi-layer codebook and coherent single-layer codebook relative to CP-OFDM with coherent single/multi-layer codebook [R1-2602254].
Dynamic waveform switching
One company observes comparable system level performance for DWS among DFT-s-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer and CP-OFDM with both 1-layer and 2-layer compared to DWS among DFT-s-OFDM for only 1-layer and CP-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer for full buffer traffic only and observes gain for non-full buffer traffic [R1-2603286].
One company observes system level loss of DFT-s-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer compared to DFT-s-OFDM for only 1-layer and CP-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer with waveform switching [R1-2601827].
One company observes comparable system level performance for DWS among DFT-s-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer and CP-OFDM with both 1-layer and 2-layer compared to DWS among DFT-s-OFDM for only 1-layer and CP-OFDM for both 1- and 2-layer. [R1-2602254].
One company observes system level performance loss of DFT-s-OFDM for 1-layer and DFT-s-OFDM/CP-OFDM for 2-layer compared to DFT-s-OFDM for only 1-layer and CP-OFDM for both 1-layer and 2-layer with waveform switching [R1-2602177].

text_en:
For GS schemes, at least the following are observed:
For 1D-NUC, if MMSE receiver is used, the demodulation/demapper complexity is [1 to 1.6] times that of uniform QAM assuming [6 to 10] quantization bit-width per I/Q for 1D-NUC.
Further observations will be worked on demodulation/demapper complexity of 1D-NUC with rML receiver
For 1D-NUC, if MMSE receiver is used, the demodulation/demapper complexity is [6.45] times that of uniform QAM assuming [14] quantization bit-width per I/Q for 1D-NUC.
Further observations will be worked on demodulation/demapper complexity of 1D-NUC with rML receiver
For 2D-NUC (except for QAM-CS), if MMSE receiver is used, the demodulation/demapper complexity is [20 to 947] times that of uniform QAM.
Further observations will be worked on demodulation/demapper complexity of QAM-CS based 2D-NUC
Further observations will be worked on demodulation/demapper complexity of 2D-NUC with rML receiver
For NP-NUC, the same demodulation/demapper as uniform QAM is used
Further observations are required to be provided for RAN plenary checkpoint to compare the complexity and storage requirements for GS with respect to uniform QAM.
Further observations of linkage between performance gain/loss under agreed fading channels with the complexity/storage are required for RAN plenary checkpoint.

For ESS based PS, the storage requirement increases approximately quadratically with increasing DM block length, the storage requirement increases exponentially with increasing number of shaped bits per I/Q symbol, and processing delay increases linearly with increasing DM block length

Further observations are required to be provided for RAN plenary checkpoint to compare the complexity and storage requirements of different DM algorithm/parameters for PS with respect to uniform QAM.
Further observations of linkage between performance gain/loss under agreed fading channels with the complexity/storage are required for RAN plenary checkpoint.

Adopt the following definition for miss detection probability and false alarm probability for RAN1 study (not intended for 6GR requirements)
Note: Definition of evaluation metrics are for the purpose of alignment of definition among companies. Companies are encouraged to provide information on evaluation metrics reported and the implication and importance of the evaluation metric in the contributions with evaluations.
Miss detection probability
Total probability of following events (for a preamble transmission):
Not detecting the preamble for a RO that was sent among the target preambles of the detecting BS
Correct preamble detection but with the wrong timing estimation
For correct preamble detection, the (residual) timing estimation error should be less than CP/2 of data symbol, e.g., SCS = 30kHz, CP/2 = 1.2 us
False alarm probability
Probability of detecting any target preamble for a RO when no transmission has occurred (only noise)
Adopt the following definition for metrics for evaluations for RAN1 study (not intended for 6GR requirements)
Note: Not all metrics may be applicable for all evaluation scenarios, and it is up to companies to provide appropriate metric(s) for information. The definitions are for the purpose of alignment of definition among companies. Companies are encouraged to provide information on evaluation metrics reported and the implication and importance of the evaluation metric in the contributions with evaluations.
Miss detection probability considering frequency estimation
Total probability of following events (for a preamble transmission):
Not detecting the preamble for a RO that was sent among the target preambles of the detecting BS
Correct preamble detection but with the wrong timing estimation and/or frequency estimation
For correct preamble detection,
the (residual) timing estimation error should be less than CP/2 of data symbol, e.g., SCS = 30kHz, CP/2 = 1.2 us, and
the (residual) frequency estimation error of PRACH detection should be less than some target value. Target value to be reported by company.
Type 1 false detection probability (intra-cell)
Probability of detecting different preamble(s) for a RO than the one that was sent among the target preambles of the detecting BS.
Type 1 false detection rate (intra-cell)
A = number of preamble(s) for a RO detected other than the one that was sent among the target preambles of the detecting BS
B = Sum of A for all ROs that contain preamble transmission
C = Total number of preamble transmission across all ROs
Type 1 false detection rate = B divided by C
Type 2 false detection probability (inter-cell)
Probability of detecting any target preamble for a RO when no transmission has occurred in the cell of detecting BS and transmission has occurred in another cell
Mixed false detection probability
Probability of detecting multiple preambles (two or more) of which one of the detected preamble is correctly detected (multiple preamble detection for the detecting BS) for a RO when only one preamble among the target preambles of the detection BS was sent.

agenda_title: Uplink transmission scheme(s) for uplink channels
text_en:
In addition to the agreement on the basic assumption of SLS for evaluation of PUSCH transmission scheme in RAN1#124, for CPE configuration, support the followings
Indoor and outdoor CPE pre-selection criterion or mechanism
Approach 0. Random selection between indoor/outdoor CPE, as baseline
(optional) Approach 1. A pre-selection criterion is applied to ensure that the CPE/FWA devices experience sufficiently good link quality and the fraction of the cell over which service is sufficiently good is reported.
(optional) Approach 2. The approach first assumes CPEs are indoors. Then according to the criteria, a number of worst performing households are either rejected or reassigned as outdoor CPEs. The number of outdoor CPEs is limited to some fraction (20% in the example of Profile 1), and the households with the worst performance that exceed the number of allowed outdoor CPEs are rejected.
In cases where CPEs are 100% indoor or outdoor, prequalification can be used, and a fraction of worst performing households are rejected.
The criteria can be e.g RSRP, minimum UL or DL data rate, etc.
Other approaches are not precluded and can be considered (reported by company if considered)
Note 1: This is only for Profile 1 (mixed deployment of indoor and outdoor CPE).
Note 2: This is also applicable for assumption of SLS for evaluation of PUSCH DMRS

agenda_title: Beam management for downlink and uplink
text_en:
For 6GR UE-initiated beam management (UEIBM), Study the following events for single-TRP as a starting point:
Event-1: The measured/predicted quality of the current/serving beam is worse than a threshold, including “beam failure”.
Event-2: The measured/predicted quality of at least one candidate beam becomes a threshold value better than the current/serving beam.
The candidate beam is associated with a same (i.e., intra-cell) or a different physical cell ID (i.e., inter-cell case) as the current/serving beam.
How to extend to m-TRP use case, including the feasibility.

Evaluation assumptions with the following clarifications
Spatial/Temporal domain DL Tx beam prediction and management, scenarios of both single-TRP and multi-TRP (intra/inter-cell) can be considered.
For multi-TRP (intra/inter-cell), companies report whether the predicted beam(s) (Set-A) are from the same set of cells/TRPs corresponding to the measured beam(s) (Set-B) or not.

Regarding frequency domain beam measurement/prediction (cross-frequency), the scenario of co-located and non-collocated, intra-frequency-range (inter-/intra-band) and inter-frequency-range can be considered.

Further clarification/extension on channel modeling (e.g., inter-frequency-range, non-collocated) can be studied.

For study of feasibility for UL WUS, at least followings are observed for DS#1b.
For the case where prior to UL WUS, always-on 6GR synchronization signals with PBCH on the standalone cell are transmitted,
UE can acquire DL timing/frequency synchronization for UL WUS transmission at least via always-on 6GR synchronization signals and PBCH transmitted by the standalone cell.
For the case where prior to UL WUS, always-on 6GR synchronization signals without PBCH on the standalone cell are transmitted,

text_en:
For the issue of HARQ stalling due to large RTT in NTN, study the following solutions (which may or may not have specification impact), including their applicability:
Solution 1: HARQ feedback disabling.
Solution 2: PDSCH / PUSCH transmissions that span multiple slots.
Solution 3: aNB reusing the same HARQ process before receiving HARQ-ACK feedback for the previous transmission
Solution 4: Sufficient number of HARQ processes
Note: Combination of solutions above can be considered.
FFS: Whether the above techniques can be harmonized with TN

text_en:
The following TP for TS 38.212 Clause 6.3.1.1.2 is endorsed.
Reason for change: For P/SP CSI reporting on PUCCH for performance monitoring, it is possible that the number of information bits of RS-PAI becomes less than 3 bits. However, NR specifications do not support PUCCH carrying 1 or 2 information bits other than HARQ-ACK/SR.
Summary of change: For P/SP CSI reporting on PUCCH for performance monitoring, the number of information bits of related CSI is zero padded to 3 bits.
Consequences if not approved: For P/SP CSI reporting on PUCCH for performance monitoring, 1-bit or 2-bit payload size of RS-PAI is not supported.
| 6.3.1.1.2 CSI only <omitted texts> If none of the CSI reports for transmission on a PUCCH is of two parts, the CSI fields of all CSI reports, in the order from upper part to lower part in Table 6.3.1.1.2-12, are mapped to the UCI bit sequence starting with . The most significant bit of each field is mapped to the lowest order information bit for that field, e.g. the most significant bit of the first field is mapped to. If the length of UCI bit sequence is less than 3 bits, zeros shall be appended to the UCI bit sequence until its length equals 3. R1-2606915 	FL summary#6 for 6G channel coding	Moderator (ZTE)
Final post-meeting summary for this agenda item.

For the study of 5G RM code for small UCI with 3~11 bits, the following are observed based on companies’ contributions:
11 sources (R1-2605455, R1-2605560, R1-2605655, R1-2605714, R1-2605783, R1-2606019, R1-2606283, R1-2606307, R1-2606308, R1-2606371, R1-2606638) observed that 5G RM code suffers from error floor and performance degradation at high code rates (e.g., R>=1/2) due to rank deficiency or limited minimum Hamming distance
On the other hand, the following are also observed:
2 sources (R1-2605288, R1-2606793) observed small UCI with 3~11 bits is generally scheduled with low code rates.
1 source (R1-2605821) observed that the rank-deficiency cases occur in approximately 6.7% of all the valid (E, K) configurations and have negligible impact on system performance.
5 sources (R1-2605288, R1-2605455, R1-2605560, R1-2605714, R1-2605783) observed that the mother code length of 5G RM code is limited to 32. Furthermore, 4 sources (R1-2605288, R1-2605455, R1-2605560, R1-2605783) observed repetition is needed at low code rates, thus the performance and coverage is degraded.  1 source (R1-2605288) observed small UCI with 3~11 bits is generally scheduled with low code rates.
4 sources (R1-2605455, R1-2605560, R1-2606308, R1-2606371) observed the BLER performance loss of 5G RM code due to DMRS overhead at least for PUCCH.
2 sources (R1-2605455, R1-2605560) observed the performance loss of 5G RM code due to high PAPR at least for PUCCH.
3 sources (R1-2605455, R1-2605560, R1-2605909) observed 5G RM code cannot support DMRS-less transmission at least for PUCCH due to the all-one vector in the first column.
In addition, the following are also observed:
4 sources (R1-2605821, R1-2606793, R1-2606769, R1-2605379) observed that RM code was used in 5G NR, and 6G does not have new requirements for this region to justify re-design.
1 source (R1-2605379) observed that 5G RM code is optimized for good minimum distance and can be decoded via FHT-based ML decoding with low complexity.
The potential solutions (coding based only) to enhance performance for small UCI with 3~11 bits are summarized as below
12 sources (R1-2605560, R1-2605655, R1-2605714, R1-2605783, R1-2605909, R1-2606793, R1-2606283, R1-2606307, R1-2606308, R1-2606371, R1-2606638, R1-2606019) discussed the potential solutions to improve the performance for short block code.
Enhanced RM code
8 sources (R1-2605560, R1-2605655, R1-2605714, R1-2605783, R1-2606793, R1-2606371, R1-2606638, R1-2606019) observed enhanced RM code with optimized basis sequence selection and/or rate matching can resolve the rank deficiency and error floor issue of RM code at high code rates.
1 source (R1-2605783) observed enhanced RM code can provide 0.7dB and 1.4dB performance gain under the case of K=3 and 4 at medium code rate respectively, resolve error floor or provide 0.7~1.2dB performance gain under the case of K=6~8 and 11 at higher code rate.
1 source (R1-2605714) observed that enhanced RM code by introducing row permutation in the basis RM sequence selection can resolve error floor under the cases of K=6~9 and 11 at higher code rate, and provide 0.52~0.57 dB performance gain under the cases of {E=12, K=6, 7} and {E=14, K=7}.
1 source (R1-2606371) observed applying an interleaver before rate matching for 5G RM code can fix the rank deficiency problem, and provide 0.1~0.9dB, 0.1~0.4dB and 0.1~0.2dB performance gain for K = 3~11, E = 12, 16 and 24, respectively.
1 source (R1-2606019) observed Kerdock code, which contains the first-order RM code, can provide 0.11dB mean performance gain, 2.62dB maximum performance gain across all combinations of (K, E).
1 source (R1-2606793) observed extension of RM code (n*32, K), n=2 or 4 can provide up to 0.6 dB performance gain in AWGN for n=4 over 5G RM code (32, K) with repetition.
1 source (R1-2605909) observed that RM (32,13) code agreed in RAN1 #52bis can provide 11 base sequences, excluding the base sequence of all-1’s.
Enhanced PC-Polar code
5 sources (R1-2605288, R1-2605560, R1-2605714, R1-2605783, R1-2605909) observed that enhanced PC-Polar code can resolve the rank deficiency and error floor issue of 5G RM code at high code rates, and improve the performance at low code rates
1 source (R1-2605909) observed about 0.7dB gain from enhanced PC-Polar code for K=8 bits and E=256 bits.
1 source (R1-2605288) observed enhanced PC-Polar code can improve the BLER performance by [0.6~0.9] dB and increase coverage by >10% over 5G RM code at low code rates, and also observed enhanced PC-Polar code can provide the benefits of error detection via parity check bits and unequal error protection for important bits.
vertical and horizontal code
1 source (R1-2606308) observed vertical and horizontal code can provide about 0.4 dB performance gain for K=8, E=12, and about 2 dB performance gain for K=8, E=26.
New code derived from linear block codes or orthogonal subspaces
1 source (R1-2606283) observed by constructing the short block length codes using sequences or using generator polynomial, the minimum hamming distance can be increased.
CRC polynomial code
1 source (R1-2606307) observed CRC polynomial code can provide better BLER performance than 5G RM code for K=6, E=8, and K=7, E=10.
Golay-based code
1 source (R1-2606371) observed Golay-based code can provide 0.1~1.0dB, 0.2~0.6dB, 0.1~0.4dB, 0.1~0.4dB and 0.2~0.3dB performance gain for K = 3~11, E= 12, 16, 20, 24 and 32, respectively.
On the other hand, 5 sources (R1-2605379, R1-2605821, R1-2606793, R1-2606769, R1-2606494) suggested reusing 5G RM code for small UCI with 3~11 bits, e.g., to avoid optimization for high coding rates that are atypical for normal usage.
2 sources (R1-2605821, R1-2605379) observed that the rank-deficiency (E, K) issue can be resolved by the scheduler through allocating a marginally larger number of coded bits without specification change.

To report the following details for PRACH evaluations:
Receiver algorithm details, including:
Detection threshold strategy:
threshold configured to address false alarm only (impacting miss detection)
Example 1) Threshold is determined based on noise variance
threshold configured to address false alarm (impacting miss detection) and false detection probability jointly
Example 2) Threshold is determined based on noise variance, inter-sequence interference + noise estimated from measurements outside the window of the detected peak
Detection metric is normalized by interference+noise estimate, where the estimate is derived (e.g., maximum or median of the detection metric) from the detection metric outside the window around the detected peak within the NCS duration of the preamble. The detection peak window can be +/- estimated/approximated channel delay.
Example 3) Threshold is determined based on noise variance, sequence interference estimated from measurement of total receive signal power of a RO
In case of ZC sequence detection with Restricted Set A and B, details of detection algorithm to handle the detection sidelobes.
For False alarm statistics, which option used for false alarm (and determination of detection threshold)
Option 1) if BS performs detection on a RO, the false alarm event happens for a preamble sequence detection, and a false alarm event is counted for the preamble sequence (false alarm event may happen multiple times within a RO for across the multiple preamble sequences). In this case, the denominator used to compute false alarm probability is the number of preambles to be detected (per RO).
Option 2) if BS performs detection on a RO, the false alarm event happens for any preamble sequence detection, and the a single false alarm event counted for a RO. In this case, denominator used to compute false alarm probability is 1 (per RO).
Relative Tx power assumption of UEs (and any pathloss measurement and RF impairment modeling, if used)
User distribution per RO, for example
Same number of users transmitting PRACH preamble in each RO
Varying number of users transmitting PRACH preamble in each RO (may be based on traffic characteristics)
Preamble sequence selection
For example, NR ZC provides information on number of root sequences, number of cyclic shifts, and Ncs value among the 64 preamble set used for evaluation.

For the potential PAPR impact and potential solutions for PAPR reduction for JSCM-based CSI compression, the following options have been studied in RAN 1, until RAN 1 #126:
Option 0: Compression outputs are directly mapped to DFT-s-OFDM or CP-OFDM uplink transmission as modulation constellation without any additional operation
Option 1: Compression outputs are mapped to certain discrete constellation, and then mapped to DFT-s-OFDM or CP-OFDM uplink transmission, at least considering the following as the discrete constellation
NR modulation constellations, e.g., 16QAM, 64QAM, 256QAM, 1024QAM
Other modulation constellations, e.g., 64APSK, constellation point pruning from NR QAM, other customized (fixed) constellations
Note: To reduce PAPR (by achieving uniform distribution of JSCM symbols), regularization can be additionally considered as part of loss function as implementation
Note: the training may or may not be aware of the mapping.
Option 2: Compression outputs are mapped/restricted, e.g., with restricted amplitude(s), and then mapped to DFT-s-OFDM or CP-OFDM uplink transmission as modulation constellation
Note: on top of Option 0/1/2, PAPR restriction during the training with or without additional activation layer, as part of loss function, can be considered.
Other solutions or potential issues related to PAPR can be further studied.

The following observations on PAPR/Cubic metric/output power variation (cross OFDM symbols) have been made for the above options at least for projection-matrix-based compression for JSCM, until RAN 1 #126:
With DFT-s-OFDM as uplink waveform,
For Option 0: 13 sources showed without any additional operation, PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% of JSCM increases by 1.5~2dB compared to conventional 16-/64-/256-QAM constellation, and ~3dB compared to conventional QPSK constellation.
4 sources showed that with Kronecker-based matrices, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% additionally increases by 1~2.5dB.
1 source showed with PAPR aware training, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is ~0.2dB lower or 0.1dB higher compared to conventional 16-QAM.
1 source showed with PAPR aware training, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is ~0.3dB lower compared to conventional 256-QAM.
1 source showed clipping aware training, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is 9dB.
1 source showed that with PAPR aware training towards 6RB, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is about ~6dB (comparable to QPSK), however, if the number of RBs used in inference is 1RB, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% increased to 8dB (i.e., 2dB higher than QPSK).
1 source showed that JSCM followed by 2-stage PAPR reduction (first stage trainable constellation mapper followed by second stage adaptive PAPR reduction block), the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% can be reduced to 4dB (PAPR = 8dB @CCDF= 0.01%).
1 source showed the cubic metric @CCDF=0.1% increases ~2.9dB compared to conventional QPSK.
1 source showed JSCM output power variation across OFDM symbols is larger than 1K-QAM PUSCH with assumption of frequency first, time second mapping of JSCM outputs to allocated REs (on to 12 subcarriers in freq domain).
For Option 1: 13 companies showed that the PAPR can be reduced but remain higher than conventional QAM
By mapping to conventional constellations, e.g., 64-QAM or 256-QAM,
13 sources showed PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% can be reduced but remain 0.2~1dB higher than conventional 64-QAM/256-QAM,
1 source showed PAPR @CCDF= 1% can be ~0.5dB lower than conventional constellation, i.e., 64-QAM/256-QAM with scaling of the compression outputs before mapping to the discrete constellations and the training is not aware of the mapping.
1 source showed with regularization as part of loss function and then mapping to 64-QAM, the PAPR is comparable to conventional 64-QAM.
2 sources showed that with Kronecker-based matrices, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is ~0.2 dB higher than conventional 64-QAM (12 subcarriers and 1024 FFT, or 12 subcarriers and 128 FFT). 1 source showed that with Kronecker-based matrices, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is ~1.5dB higher than conventional 64-QAM (64 subcarriers with 2048-FFT).
1 source showed, that varying the number of Resource Elements (REs) impacts the PAPR:
Dedicated model: with 32 REs, the PAPR at CCDF = 0.1% can be ~0.5 dB lower than that of a conventional 64-QAM constellation. However, with 48 or 64 REs, the PAPR is either comparable to or ~0.3 dB higher than conventional 64-QAM.
Scalable model: With 32 REs, the PAPR is comparable to conventional 64-QAM. However, with 48 or 64 REs, the PAPR at CCDF = 0.1% can be ~0.7 dB or 1.8 dB higher, respectively, than conventional 64-QAM.
1 source showed that different loss functions during training may lead to differences in the statistical distribution/probability of the mapped constellation points from the compression outputs. Specifically, the PAPR @ CCDF = 0.1% might vary by 0.3 dB to 1 dB.
By mapping to other modulation constellations,
1 source showed with mapping to 64APSK, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is 0.2 dB higher than conventional 64-QAM.
2 sources showed with mapping to constellation point pruning from NR QAM, PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is comparable or up to 1dB lower comparing to conventional constellation, i.e., 64-QAM or 256-QAM.
For Option 2: By mapping/restricting, some companies showed that the PAPR can be reduced to comparable to conventional QPSK or 16-QAM
4 sources showed with mapping to constant amplitude, PAPR is comparable to conventional QPSK and 2 sources showed PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is ~0.5dB lower than conventional QPSK.
2 sources showed with mapping to annular constellation, with scaling factor = 0.5, the PAPR is comparable to conventional 16-QAM.
1 source showed that with mapping to annular constellation, with dense matrix or with Kronecker-based matrices, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is reduced to 8.5dB.
1 source showed with both the maximum and minimum amplitudes, the PAPR @CCDF= 1% is comparable to conventional QPSK. And with peak limited only, the PAPR @CCDF= 1% is ~0.4dB higher than conventional 16-QAM.
Note: no multiplexing with other UL transmission is assumed in the above evaluation.
Note: 12 to 72 of subcarriers are assumed with 128, 1024 or 2048 or 4096 FFT size.
With CP-OFDM as uplink waveform,
For Option 0(without and additional operation) and. for Option 1, by mapping to conventional constellations, e.g., 64-QAM or 256-QAM,
5 sources showed the PAPR of JSCM is comparable to conventional 16-/64-/256-QAM.
1 source showed for 1 RB, the PAPR @CCDF= 0.1% is 1dB higher than conventional 16-/64-/256-QAM.
1 source showed the cubic metric @CCDF=0.1% increases ~1.9dB compared to conventional QPSK
For Option 1,
By mapping to conventional constellations, e.g., 64-QAM or 256-QAM,
4 sources showed the PAPR of JSCM is comparable to conventional 16-/64-/256-QAM.
By mapping to other modulation constellations,
1 source showed with mapping to constellation point pruning from NR QAM, PAPR is comparable conventional QPSK, or conventional 16-/64-/256-QAM.
For Option 2: By mapping/restricting,
1 source showed with mapping to constant amplitude or annular constellation the PAPR is comparable to conventional QPSK/16-QAM.
1 source showed with both the maximum and minimum amplitudes, the PAPR @CCDF= 1% is about 7.2dB (2.8dB lower than conventional QPSK). And with peak limited only, the PAPR is comparable to conventional QPSK/16QAM.
Note: no multiplexing with other UL transmission is assumed in the above evaluation.
Note: 12 to 72 of subcarriers is assumed with 1024 or 2048 FFT size.
Note: in the above observations, for conventional modulations for both DFT-s-OFDM and CP-OFDM waveform, no additional PAPR reduction technique is considered.
Note: the observation can be further updated based on new results in future meetings.

Quantized buffer size.

UE reports the time information corresponding to the measurement resource with the largest RSRP/RSSI measurement.

text_en:

DL WUS processing timeline relaxation

On the issue of HARQ stalling, the following observations are drawn:
On Solution 1 (HARQ feedback disabling) and Solution 3 (aNB reusing the same HARQ process before receiving HARQ-ACK feedback for the previous transmission):
RAN1 observes that solution 1 was specified in NR Rel-17, and it is clarified in TS 38.300 that “Disabling HARQ feedback allows scheduling a HARQ process before one HARQ RTT has elapsed since last scheduled”. This solution is feasible from RAN1 perspective
From RAN1 perspective, regarding Solution 3, it is feasible to allow usage of the same HARQ process before the HARQ-ACK feedback has been processed by the base station (subject to out-of-order rules at the UE). Current RAN2 specifications for NR, however, may prevent this behavior at least in some cases (e.g. when DRX is configured).
Under solution 3, having HARQ-ACK feedback for every downlink transmission incurs in signaling overhead and corresponding UE power consumption, which is considered by some companies to be unacceptable for some NTN scenarios. Solution 1 would alleviate this issue.
Some companies indicate that the UE power consumption and overhead associated with HARQ-ACK transmission is limited, and that solution 1 removes the information on successful or unsuccessful reception of the TB and may result in recovery through RLC retransmissions which would increase signaling overhead, latency and corresponding UE power consumption. This assumes that, under solution 3, HARQ-ACK information is used for ARQ retransmissions without relying on RLC status report.
Some companies indicate that although Solution 3 does not remove the information on successful or unsuccessful reception of the TB, it will not be useful for triggering HARQ retransmissions, and therefore with solution 3 there is also a possibility of ending up in recovery through RLC retransmissions. This assumes that, under solution 3, HARQ-ACK information is not used for ARQ retransmissions without relying on RLC status report.
Under solution 3, although HARQ-ACK feedback is not used for HARQ retransmissions, some companies indicate that the HARQ-ACK information can be useful for e.g. link adaptation. Some other companies indicate that similar information can be conveyed in an alternative manner (e.g. statistical reporting, dynamic enabling/disabling of HARQ feedback under Solution 1, or disabling of HARQ feedback for some of the HARQ processes).
Some companies indicate that the potential benefits of solution 1 in terms of signaling efficiency and power consumption are not directly related to HARQ stalling. Some companies indicate that solution 1 has been specified in NR to solve the problem of HARQ stalling.
NOTE: The fact that solution 3 and solution 1 are deemed to be “feasible” has no impact on which solution (if any) would be specified.

Reason for change: In Rel-19, UEIRI is introduced as a new type of UCI for notifying (ModeA) or requesting a PUSCH resource (ModeB) for UE-initiated/event-driven beam reporting. Whether UE transmits UEIRI on a PUCCH format 0 or format 1 in the PUCCH resource depends on whether the triggering condition of the event(s) for UE-initiated/event-driven beam reporting is met or not. In this case, the information bit of UEIRI is not always included in the PUCCH resource. However, in the current spec, UEIRI is described as a compulsory UCI in the PUCCH resource, which is not correct.
Summary of change: Add the condition “if any” to the information bit for UEIRI where the contents of UCI bit(s) are described in the first paragraph of Section 9.2, TS38.213.
Consequences if not approved: The availability of information bit for UEIRI in PUCCH is not correctly stated.
| 9.2 UCI reporting in physical uplink control channel UCI types reported in a PUCCH include HARQ-ACK information, SR, LRR, UEIRI, and CSI. UCI bits include HARQ-ACK information bits, if any, SR information bits, if any, LRR information bit, if any, UEIRI information bit, if any, and CSI bits, if any. The HARQ-ACK information bits correspond to a HARQ-ACK codebook as described in clause 9.1. For the remaining of this clause, unless stated otherwise in clauses 9.2.4A and 9.2.5.1, any reference to SR is applicable for SR and/or for LRR and/or for UEIRI. <Unchanged parts are omitted> |

| Reason for change: The periodicity of on-demand SSB can be configured differently than the always-on SSB. However, the current spec says the UE can assume a periodicity of a half frame when the always-on SSB periodicity parameter is absent. When the on-demand SSB periodicity is different than the always-on SSB periodicity this then conflicts with the following statement in the spec which says the UE can assume the periodicity of all SS/PBCH blocks in the serving cell is the same. Summary of Change: Clarify that the assumption of the same periodicity from all SS/PBCH blocks in the serving cell does not hold for on-demand SSB. Consequences if not approved: Incorrect UE assumption on the periodicity of the SSB. 4.1 Cell search < Unchanged Text Omitted > A UE can be provided per serving cell by ssb-periodicityServingCell a periodicity of the half frames for reception of the SS/PBCH blocks for the serving cell. If the UE is not configured a periodicity of the half frames for receptions of the SS/PBCH blocks, the UE assumes a periodicity of a half frame. A UE assumes that the periodicity is same for all SS/PBCH blocks in the serving cell, expect for SS/PBCH blocks provided by OD-SSB-Config, as described in Clause 4.4. < Unchanged Text Omitted > |

| Reason for change: | In NB-IoT NTN TDD operation, it was concluded to do not “specify further enhancements for NPUSCH format 1 scheduling delays”. This was adopted based on the understanding that legacy scheduling values (8, 16, 32, 64) can be used under the assumption that if the scheduled uplink transmission falls into a guard period subframe (muted subframe) then the most immediate available subframe is used. However, this assumption/behavior is currently not described into the 3GPP technical specifications. |

| Summary of change: | Incorporating in clause 16.5.1 of TS 36.213 for NB-IoT NTN TDD operation, a statement that aligns terminology of legacy procedures (i.e., “a slot is considered an NB-IoT UL slot if is it fully contained within an NB-IoT UL subframe”) to reflect that if because of the scheduling delay value the NPUSCH format 1 transmission happens to coincide with a guard period subframe, then the NPUSCH format 1 transmission shall be performed at the first available subframe of the U consecutive uplink subframes of NB-IoT NTN TDD operation. |
|  |  |
| Consequences if not approved: | If the behavior is not described, there is no guarantee that all implementations will have to assume that a scheduled uplink transmission that falls into a guard period subframes should be understood to be postponed to the most immediate available uplink subframe. |

Capture the following in the Draft LS response to R1-2605188.
The misalignment between transmission of PRACH at UE side and monitoring of PRACH at NW side may occur in beam hopping operation when RO periodicity is <160ms. Some companies have the view that the misalignment is due to configuration or NW implementation.
The misalignment may also occur in beam hopping operation when RO periodicity is 160ms and cells served by the same hopping beam have overlapping valid PRACH occasions, e.g. due to the aligned SFN and same PRACH time-domain configuration and SSB-to-RO mapping, while the corresponding satellite Rx beam is not active for a footprint at such PRACH occasions.
The draft LS in R1-2606882 is endorsed by changing “kindly” to “respectfully”.
The final LS in R1-2606892 is approved.
